title: When the Orbit Falls
premise: Wendell Oyelaran has spent eleven years alone tending Earth's derelict seed vault, keeping a beacon alive for a world that stopped listening. When she finds her own name—misspelled, then corrected—on the manifest of the Meridian, a ship that never launched, she realizes someone is rewriting records to erase people, and she is next. Pursued by an Auditor who deletes rather than arrests, Wendell flees with two stowaways: a boy who remembers a mother he never had, and a disgraced archivist who knows how the erasure machine works. Their race to the dead-space relay becomes a fight to broadcast proof of every deleted life before the vault's failing reactor—and the Auditor's countdown—reaches zero. In the end Wendell chooses to stay behind and hold the transmission open, becoming not the forgotten caretaker but the voice everyone remembers.
about_author: Freya Thackeray is a former radio astronomer who left academia after a funding scandal erased her research team's work from public record. She writes from a converted lighthouse on the Atlantic coast, where she still keeps one transmitter running out of principle.

chapters.title: The Quiet Inventory
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. A day in the seed vault: checking germination trays, logging frost damage, singing to the beacon so its signal stays warm. The rhythm of solitude is broken when the manifest terminal prints a name that shouldn't exist. Emotional beat: loneliness revealed as devotion, then pierced by unease.

chapters.title: A Ship That Never Flew
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. She digs into the Meridian's manifest and finds forty names, each one scrubbed from every other database she can reach—including, as of last night, her own. Emotional beat: the vertigo of discovering your existence is negotiable.

chapters.title: The Boy in Bay Four
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. Investigating a power drain, she finds Tam, a stowaway child hiding among cryo-spares, clutching memories of a mother whose records also don't exist. He remembers things about the vault he couldn't know. Emotional beat: reluctant tenderness; two invisible people recognizing each other.

chapters.title: Signal Ghosts
chapters.summary: Tam's POV. Through his fragmented memories we see the erasure at work: faces going smooth, doors that were never there. He believes Wendell can 'un-delete' his mother. Emotional beat: grief worn as certainty, and the weight of being believed.

chapters.title: The Archivist
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. A battered shuttle crash-lands near the vault carrying Ilsa Reyes-Mbeki, former Records Authority, now fugitive, carrying a stolen decryption key for the deletion engine. She came looking for the beacon's origin. Emotional beat: wary alliance forged from mutual desperation.

chapters.title: What the Beacon Was For
chapters.summary: Ilsa's POV. Decrypted files reveal the beacon was built to preserve a master index of every citizen—a backup against exactly this kind of erasure—and that its commissioning order bears Wendell's true name. Emotional beat: the shock of learning you were chosen before you chose.

chapters.title: Arrival of the Auditor
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. A sleek enforcement vessel enters orbit. Its passenger, Auditor Voss, broadcasts a polite request to surrender 'misplaced assets.' The reactor, aging and unstable, begins an automatic safety countdown triggered by the ship's scan. Emotional beat: dread arriving with perfect courtesy.

chapters.title: Forty Names
chapters.summary: Ilsa's POV. Reading the manifest aloud, they give the deleted their histories back—Tam's mother among them. Tam finally hears his mother described by someone else and breaks. Emotional beat: mourning as an act of resistance.

chapters.title: The Long Launch
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. They strip the vault's reserve fuel into Ilsa's shuttle and launch during a sensor shadow, leaving the beacon running on fumes. Voss lets them go—too easily. Emotional beat: escape shadowed by the suspicion of a trap.

chapters.title: Dead Space
chapters.summary: Tam's POV. Aboard the shuttle, the void between relays stretches silent. Tam teaches Wendell the star-charts his mother sang to him; she realizes the songs are navigation data—the deleted knew this route. Emotional beat: found family forming in the dark.

chapters.title: The Trap at Relay Nine
chapters.summary: Ilsa's POV. Relay Nine is manned—or appears to be. It's a decoy broadcasting false safety signals while Voss's drones close in. Ilsa sacrifices the shuttle's drive to buy distance, stranding them on a drifting relay segment. Emotional beat: guilt and grit; the cost of trust.

chapters.title: Countdown
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. With the vault reactor at T-minus sixty hours and Voss's deletion sweep inbound, Wendell works out the brutal math: only the relay's transmitter has the range to reach the master index, but it needs a power source bigger than anything aboard. Emotional beat: clarity through crisis.

chapters.title: The Key and the Lie
chapters.summary: Ilsa confesses her decryption key is half-forged; she was the one who designed the deletion engine before defecting. Tam overhears. Emotional beat: betrayal, then the harder question—who gets to be forgiven?

chapters.title: Voss's Offer
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. Voss hails them directly: surrender the key and Tam, and the vault will be spared, its history rewritten kindly. Wendell hears the seduction of a clean story. Emotional beat: temptation of comfortable forgetting.

chapters.title: What Tam Remembers
chapters.summary: Tam's POV. Under pressure, Tam's fractured memories resolve: his mother wasn't deleted randomly—she discovered the erasure program first, and hid the completion codes inside a lullaby. The song is the missing half of Ilsa's key. Emotional beat: a child's inheritance becoming the weapon.

chapters.title: Sixty Hours
chapters.summary: Ilsa's POV. They rebuild the relay's transmitter from salvage while Voss's drones pick through the debris field. Ilsa and Tam reconcile over the work; Wendell plans something she tells no one. Emotional beat: fragile unity under a ticking clock.

chapters.title: The Broadcast
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. They transmit the restored index—forty lives, then thousands—piggybacked on the old beacon frequency so it cannot be blocked without admitting the beacon existed. Voss's ship powers weapons. Emotional beat: defiant joy curdling into terror.

chapters.title: Zero Hour
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. The vault reactor hits zero just as the transmission needs one final surge. Wendell reroutes herself into the relay's systems manually, holding the channel open with her own body as interface, buying the seconds the broadcast requires. Emotional beat: sacrifice chosen freely, fear and purpose intertwined.

chapters.title: The Signal That Would Not Die
chapters.summary: Tam's POV. From the shuttle, Tam narrates the broadcast reaching colony after colony—names read back, families recognizing the deleted. Voss's authority collapses as the lie becomes unsustainably large. Emotional beat: vindication arriving like dawn.

chapters.title: Aftermath
chapters.summary: Ilsa's POV. Rescue ships arrive. Ilsa surrenders to testify, taking responsibility for the engine she built. Tam refuses to leave without Wendell. Emotional beat: justice outside the law—accountability chosen, not imposed.

chapters.title: The Voice in the Vault
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. Wendell survived, changed—partially merged with the relay, able to speak across any frequency. She chooses to remain at the vault, now a living archive, with Tam staying as her hands and eyes. Emotional beat: home redefined; invisibility transformed into presence.

chapters.title: When the Orbit Falls
chapters.summary: Tam's POV, years later. The vault is a pilgrimage site; the beacon sings every name nightly. Tam, now a keeper-in-training, adds new entries to the manifest—not deletions, but births. Emotional beat: memory as inheritance, and the quiet triumph of being remembered.
